newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries end up after Fed holds line on rates - Sept 24.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries end up after Fed holds line on rates - Sept 24.

text.p: U.S. Treasury securities prices ended higher on Tuesday after the Federal Reserve decided not to lift interest rates.

The decision mildly surprised the market where many had thought recent wage gains and a low unemployment rate were forerunners of inflation that would persuade Fed officials to raise rates at Tuesday's much anticipated policy meeting.
In the half hour before the Fed released its statement, prices climbed about a third of a point from levels that had been nearly unchanged on the day.

On news the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) left rates untouched, the market doubled that gain then receded. The bellwether 30-year bond rose 3/4 point, then cut its gain to end at 97-1/32, up 14/32, to yield 6.99 percent.

"The kneejerk reaction was the simple one in which the market rallied to news that rates are going to be held steady for a time but then prices backed down from their peaks on the thought that the Fed is doing experiments with inflation and that it's not as vigilant on inflation as perhaps it should be," said Michael Moran, chief economist at Daiwa Securities America Inc.

Short-term bill rates, which are most responsive to near-term Fed policy adjustments, fell sharply as prospects for higher official interest rates receded at least until the Fed's next policy meeting in November, analysts said.
Three- and six-month Treasury bill rates fell 20 basis points and 14 basis points, respectively, closing at 4.97 percent and 5.15 percent.
"This puts us right back to square zero with people handicapping what November's meeting will result in," said economist Neal Soss, senior advisor to CS First Boston Corp.
"You'll be dealing with a 5-1/4 percent Federal funds rate until November at the earliest," said Kevin Flanagan, first vice president and money market economist at Dean Witter Reynolds Inc.

Samuel Kahan, president of A.S.K. Financial Research Ltd., said the Fed had relied on "the basic assumption that the economic numbers are suffiently mixed that a case can be made for the economy's moderation in the future."
Kahan said that "if one believes the retail sales reports, it looks like third-quarter GDP (gross domestic product) will come in around two- or 2.5 percent or so."
Second-half GDP growth of two percent or less would probably assuage most inflation concerns in the market.
Kahan said the second element of the Fed's decision to hold rates steady is that so far, inflation has not accelerated.

"There may be fear of inflation, but the most telling feature is that the core CPI (Consumer Price Index) and the other general price indicators have remained virtually unchanged despite the fact that the unemployment rate has been below the six-percent mark for two years and is now almost a full percentage point below that at 5.1 percent," Kahan said.
Elliott Platt, managing director, economic research at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette, said the big risk to the market now is the arrival of stronger-than-anticipated economic data.
Platt, himself, expects upcoming reports on durable goods orders, new home sales and September payroll growth to be subdued.
Anything contrary to that would set the market back, he said.

"That's the big risk," Platt said. "Let's say the September payrolls report is strong and the next CPI is up 0.3 percent. The market could have a horrible case of indigestion which would have been mitigated by some sort of pre-emptive rate hike by the Fed. But the Fed apparently thinks it's a risk worth taking."

At the close, the year bill rate was down 12 basis points to 5.40 percent. The two-year note was up 6/32 to 99-31/32, yielding 6.14 percent, the five-year note up 12/32 at 99-31/32, yielding 6.51 percent and the 10-year note up 15/32 at 101-24/32 to yield 6.75 percent. -- 212-859-1679
